standard_prerequisites.name: HF-ordering
standard_prerequisites.statement: A linear ordering in which every element has at most one pair of smaller elements forming a block with it.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is what the cited proposition supplies for an unconfined system.

standard_prerequisites.name: Elementary substructure
standard_prerequisites.statement: A$\leq$B means that A is an elementary substructure of B, so that the closure conditions transfer.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the relation appearing in the second item.

standard_prerequisites.name: Inherited ordering
standard_prerequisites.statement: A subset of an ordered structure inherits the ordering, and the initial segment condition restricts to it.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the mechanism of the second item.

core_obligations: For the first item, apply the cited proposition, since every unconfined system has an HF-ordering (source line 657).

For the second item, start from an HF-ordering of B having A2 as an initial segment and restrict it to A1, which gives an HF-ordering of A1 whose initial segment is the intersection of the two (source line 659).

proof_roadmap.step: First item follows from the existence of an HF-ordering.
Second item by restricting an HF-ordering to A1.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 650-655, which has two items: the empty set is below every unconfined system, and if B is unconfined and contains A1 while A2 is elementary in B, then the intersection of A1 and A2 is elementary in A1. The first item is immediate from the cited existence of an HF-ordering. The second (source line 659) is the substantive half and is where the diamond shape appears: one takes an HF-ordering of B with A2 as an initial segment and restricts it to A1, so that the inherited ordering has exactly the intersection as its initial segment. The statement records the two items and neither the choice of ordering nor the restriction step.
